name: Think-on-Graph

paper.title: Think-on-Graph: Deep and Responsible Reasoning of Large Language Model on Knowledge Graph

construction.unit: knowledge-graph triple (head entity, relation, tail entity) reached during the search
construction.kept_as: verbatim KG triples: entity names and raw relation ids
construction.processing: nothing is written ahead of time; per question, the top 3 triples of each search depth are appended to a working list
construction.writer: none: the KG (Freebase or Wikidata) is pre-built and read-only

organization.structure: external knowledge graph, plus a flat per-question list of kept triples
organization.stores: Freebase behind a SPARQL endpoint, or Wikidata behind nine API calls; the triple list lives only in the prompt
organization.index: entity ids (Freebase mid, Wikidata qid) looked up by fixed SPARQL/API queries

management.operations: append up to 3 triples per depth; their tail entities become the next frontier; the KG itself is never changed by the system

retrieval.query: the question, starting from topic entities supplied with the dataset (paper: extracted by the LLM)
retrieval.candidates: all relations of each frontier entity (minus type/common/freebase/sameAs), then the tail entities of the chosen relations (5 sampled at random if 20 or more)
retrieval.selection: LLM picks and scores 3 relations per entity, LLM scores the tail entities; a triple scores relation × entity and the top 3 overall are kept; an LLM check after each depth decides whether to stop
retrieval.budget: width N=3, depth D=3: at most 9 triples; at most 2ND+D+1 = 22 LLM calls per question (paper)

use.context: the question and all kept triples as "head, relation, tail" lines, with 5 in-context examples
use.reasoning: the sufficiency reply also states the answer when it says Yes; if depth 3 ends without Yes, a CoT prompt answers without any triples

classify.note: Memory here is an existing knowledge graph that the system only reads. The per-question triple list only grows; the LLM scores decide which neighbours are kept, and a fixed rule keeps the top 3.

stages.organization: Knowledge lives in an existing KG (Freebase for CWQ, WebQSP, GrailQA, SimpleQuestions and WebQuestions; Wikidata for the other four sets); ToG only reads it.
stages.update: During one question, each search depth appends its top 3 triples to a working list whose tail entities seed the next depth.
stages.retrieval: From the topic entities, fixed SPARQL queries list neighbouring relations; the LLM keeps 3 per entity with scores, the tails of those relations are fetched and scored by the LLM, and the 3 triples with the highest relation × entity score are kept. An LLM check after each depth (at most 3) decides whether the triples suffice.
stages.answer: When the check says Yes, its reply (with the answer in braces) is the output; if 3 depths pass without Yes the LLM answers by chain-of-thought with no triples.

summary: An LLM walks a knowledge graph by beam search, choosing relations and entities at each hop and stopping when it judges the collected triples sufficient; it needs no training and works with Freebase or Wikidata.

abstract.text: Think-on-Graph (ToG) lets an LLM take part in reasoning over a knowledge graph instead of only translating a question into a query. Starting from the question's topic entities, the LLM repeatedly picks promising relations and neighbouring entities, keeping the best few paths in a beam, until it judges the gathered triples enough to answer. The method needs no training and can be paired with different LLMs and graphs. Across nine knowledge-intensive datasets it sets a new best result on six with GPT-4, and the explicit paths let people trace and correct faulty facts.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: Nothing is written: memory is an existing KG, and the LLM only decides which neighbouring relations and entities to follow.
The answer model sees at most 9 triples (3 per depth, 3 depths) as a flat list; if it never says the list is enough, it answers from its own knowledge with no triples.
In the released code the start entities come from the dataset (gold-linked ids), not from LLM extraction as the paper says.

paper_vs_code.code: read from the dataset's topic_entity field; for CWQ 3,520 of 3,531 of these ids appear in the gold SPARQL

paper_vs_code.paper: each prune step needs at most N LLM calls
paper_vs_code.code: one entity-scoring call per chosen relation, so up to N × N = 9 calls per depth
if a relation has 20 or more tails, 5 are sampled at random before the LLM sees them

paper_vs_code.paper: a separate generation call after a positive evaluation (Alg. 1, App. E.3.4)
paper_vs_code.code: the Yes reply of the evaluation prompt already contains the answer and is returned; the generate prompt runs only when a depth finds no new triples

paper_vs_code.paper: top-N reasoning paths of growing length
paper_vs_code.code: a flat list of triples, 3 per depth; triples of different paths are not linked into chains

eval.py compares the text in the first braces with the gold answers by substring in either direction; for replies from the sufficiency check that text is 'Yes' (a helper that takes the second braces is defined but not called)

open_questions: Topic entities in the released data are gold-linked ids, so the reported scores do not include entity-linking errors that a system extracting entities itself would face.
About 20% of correct answers come from the LLM's own knowledge alone (App. B.2), and every run that ends at depth 3 answers without triples; the paper does not report how often that fallback fires.

No run compares ToG with a plain retriever that feeds the same number of KG triples to the LLM, so the value of LLM-guided pruning over retrieval is shown only against BM25/SentenceBERT pruning inside ToG (Table 5).

discussion.takeaway: Letting the LLM choose each hop on a knowledge graph, and stop when it judges the evidence enough, beats both LLM-only prompting and fixed KG retrieval without training; with GPT-4 it matches or beats fine-tuned systems on most of nine sets.

claims.claim: Tight LLM-KG coupling (the LLM reasons on the graph) beats using the LLM only to write queries.
claims.evidence: §1, Fig. 1; no direct head-to-head with a query-generation system beyond KB-BINDER numbers (Table 1).

claims.claim: Best result on 6 of 9 datasets without training.
claims.evidence: With GPT-4: WebQSP 82.6, GrailQA 81.4, QALD10-en 54.7 (ToG-R), WebQuestions 57.9, Zero-Shot RE 88.3, Creak 95.6, each above the cited prior SOTA. Table 1, §3.2.1

claims.claim: Larger gains over the LLM alone on multi-hop questions.
claims.evidence: GrailQA +51.8 and Zero-Shot RE +42.9 over prompting without KG; gains over CoT grow with question depth (App. B.2, Fig. 13). §3.2.1

claims.claim: A small LLM with ToG can beat a large LLM alone.
claims.evidence: Llama-2-70B ToG-R 57.6 CWQ vs GPT-4 CoT 46.0. Table 2, §3.2.2

claims.claim: The LLM is the best pruner.
claims.evidence: BM25 or SentenceBERT pruning drops CWQ by 8.4 and WebQSP by 15.1 points on average. Table 5

claims.claim: Explicit paths make answers traceable and let users correct KG errors.

limits: Computation grows with depth and width; the paper keeps both at 3 and lists ways to cut LLM calls (App. B.2.1).
Accuracy depends on KG quality and coverage; Wikidata search and pruning are harder than Freebase for these sets (§3.2.3).
Single-hop sets gain less than multi-hop ones (§3.2.1).
Remaining errors are hallucinations and refusals; longer paths add a few format errors (App. B.2).
discussion.limits_src: paper §3.2, App. B.2 (no separate limitations section)
reading: The released code starts from topic entities stored in the data files; for CWQ these are the ids in the gold SPARQL, which removes entity linking from the task.

Table 1 and Table 2 disagree on which of ToG and ToG-R scored what: on CWQ with ChatGPT Table 1 gives ToG 57.1 / ToG-R 58.9 but Table 2 gives ToG 58.9 / ToG-R 57.1 (same swap with GPT-4, 67.6 / 69.5). Table 10 follows Table 1; our results file uses Table 1.
Llama-2 WebQSP numbers differ between Table 2 (ToG-R 68.9, ToG 63.7) and Table 11 (69.4, 64.1).
The Table 1 footnote credits CWQ's prior FT SOTA 70.4 to Das et al. (2021), but Tables 2 and 10 give that 70.4 to DecAF and 67.1 to CBR-KBQA (Das et al.).
Ablations (Tables 3-6) use 1,000-question subsets, so their full-system numbers (58.8 CWQ) differ from Table 1.

The released eval script matches by substring and takes the text in the first braces, which for replies from the sufficiency check is 'Yes'; the paper's numbers therefore cannot have come from that script unchanged.
IO, CoT and SC baselines use 6 examples; ToG reasoning prompts use 5.
